analysis.one_liner: Forces members of Congress to divest or blind-trust their individual stocks, with fines for noncompliance.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a Senate committee and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Ethics in Government Act to bar members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependents from owning individual stocks, commodities, futures, or similar financial instruments while serving in Congress, and for 180 days after leaving. Members would have to sell those assets or place them in an independently managed, government-approved blind trust, and would owe a fine equal to one month's salary for every 30 days of noncompliance. Regular diversified mutual funds, index ETFs, and Treasury bonds would still be allowed.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public. It removes the conflict of interest in which members of Congress make laws and oversee agencies while their own families hold individual stocks in the industries those decisions affect. Certification documents, trust agreements, and any fines would be posted publicly.

how_it_helps.text: Within 120 days of taking effect, current members and, within 120 days of taking office, new members would have to divest covered investments or place them in a qualified blind trust, covering their spouses and dependents as well.

The restriction would cover securities, commodities, futures, and synthetic exposure such as options and derivatives, and would last through service plus 180 days after it ends, closing the window for trades timed around insider knowledge of legislation.
Members who fail to certify or comply would face a civil penalty equal to their monthly congressional salary, assessed 30 days after notice and then at least every 30 days until they comply.
Ethics offices would have to publish certifications, blind trust agreements, asset schedules, granted extensions, and any penalties on a public website.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses with individual securities, who would have to sell them or hand them to an independent trustee and lose direct control of those investments for their entire tenure plus 180 days. Forced sales could carry transaction and tax costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress with stock holdings

drawbacks.text: The penalty is a recurring fine of one month's salary, not criminal liability, and enforcement depends entirely on the congressional ethics offices acting on their own.

Members could delay compliance with extensions of up to 180 days total, and spouses could keep assets from a non-congressional career until placed in trust, so the prohibition is not immediate or absolute in every case.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the real cost to members' families: losing control of personal investments, possibly selling at an inconvenient time, and bearing tax and transaction costs of divestiture.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall narrowly on a small group — sitting lawmakers and their households — while the benefit, removing the ability of legislators to trade individual securities in industries they regulate and legislate, is structural and permanent. The enforcement teeth are modest (a salary-sized fine rather than criminal penalty), so the bill's strength is the outright ownership bar, not the punishment. On balance a reasonable design for the problem it addresses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on January 12, 2022, and sat there with no committee vote and no floor action until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Ossoff, joined by Senator Mark Kelly, introduced the bill on January 12, 2022.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
Fifteen Democratic senators cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no further steps — no committee markup, no calendar placement, no floor vote — between the referral and the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress: the ban never came to a vote, so they kept the ability to hold and trade individual stocks, commodities, and derivatives while in office, and no new penalties or public disclosures took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent members who kept trading stocks

against.name: Sen. Gary Peters
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee where the bill was referred, never brought it to a committee vote; the bill saw no action after referral.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Publicly promised a floor vote on congressional stock-trading legislation in 2022 but never scheduled one for any version of the ban.

against.name: Rep. Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Initially resisted a broad member stock-trading ban, saying members should be able to trade, then backed a narrower disclosure-focused approach instead of a full divestiture requirement.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never reached a roll call, so no recorded votes show how parties would have split; widely reported resistance came from Democratic leadership in both chambers.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their households' individual stock portfolios
industries.note: The bill would bar members, spouses, and dependents from owning individual securities, commodities, futures, and derivatives during service plus 180 days, requiring divestiture or a qualified blind trust. Their financial interest in keeping those holdings ran directly against the public's interest in lawmakers not trading on policy knowledge, and the bill died without a vote, so the interest prevailed.
